1582.dq: previous reports have disagreed concerning the most important acoustic correlates of stress. This disagreement is largely attributable to the failure of some studies to properly differentiate between lexical stress and intonational pitch accent ... the pitch accent can be characterized as a sharp rise in f0 occurring in close alignment with the syllable bearing primary lexical stress.
1582.dloc: 'Acoustic correlates of stress and pitch accent', p.127, first fragment; 'Intonation and stress' > 'Intonation', p.119, second fragment ('In general, the pitch accent can be characterized as...')
1582.prule: Primary lexical stress usually penultimate; antepenultimate in roots with a 'weak final syllable' (-na, -ka, -tra), final in some roots (e.g. atỳ 'here', lalao 'play'); membership in the weak-final class is not predictable from the segments and stress is stated to be unpredictable and distinctive (àty/atỳ, tànana/tanàna). Prefixes never shift stress; suffixes shift it rightward to the syllable before the suffix (Adelaar 2012); bimoraic enclitics attract primary stress; compounds/reduplication: primary on rightmost member/copy.
1582.srule: In words of four or more morae, secondary stress on every second mora preceding the primary-stressed syllable (Erwin 1996: 8 as reported by Howe, e.g. ˌtraoˈtraoka, ˌmilaˈlao), which Howe hedges: 'It is easy to find exceptions to this stated rule'. Demoted primaries also surface as secondary: the original root stress under reduplication (rightmost copy primary), the stressed morae of non-final compound members, and the root stress when a bimoraic enclitic (=nao) takes primary stress.

evidence_works.detail: Stress placement is cited, not observed: the §2.2 paragraph (p.201) attributes the three positions and the minimal pair [ˈla.la.na] 'road' / [laˈla.na] 'law' to O'Neill 2015 [12], the post-lexical analysis to Albro 2005 [1], and the epenthetic extrametrical final vowel to Albro 2005 and Raoniarisoa 1990 [17]. First-hand part: f0 contours measured on 118 read declarative utterances (20 sentences) from six Central Highlands speakers (five male, one female; Official Malagasy, Antananarivo 2018), with the final word of predicate and subject varied in stress position (final, penultimate, antepenultimate) to separate pitch accents from boundary tones (pp.201-202). Finding: 'a rising pitch accent appears on the rightmost stressed syllable of each ip, though the realization of this tone varies' (p.203); the rising tone 'does show similarity to pitch accents' but 'is not prominent (a result which is consistent with the perception study in [17])', so it is labelled l*+h rather than a postlexical pitch accent (p.203). This refines the entry's tone note (the L+H* accent docking on the primary-stressed syllable) and touches no stress coding.

evidence_works.work: Albro 2005, Studies in Computational Optimality Theory, with Special Reference to the Phonological System of Malagasy (PhD dissertation, UCLA: pp. 93, 123, 134-135, 211)
evidence_works.detail: Merina ('the standard dialect'). An implemented OT grammar checked by computer against 'a database of 509 Malagasy forms, each chosen to illustrate some aspect of the sound pattern of Malagasy' (p.93); the author states 'I have relied for data and generalizations primarily on Erwin (1995), Paul (1995), Hollanger (1973), and Keenan & Polinsky (1998)' (p.93), so the forms are drawn from prior descriptions while the argument is his own. Three points, all agreeing with the entry: (a) 'The general stress pattern for Malagasy is right-to-left trochaic with the rightmost stress of a word having special prominence' (p.123), argued from the polymorphemic forms in table (17) with two secondary stresses (mi͵fampi͵rahaˈraha 'work together', mi͵faŋkaˈtia 'love each other') 'against an analysis in which the primary stress is assigned to the penultimate syllable and secondary stresses are assigned in trochees from left to right' (p.123) -- this is the same right-to-left rule the entry's `sec_quote` gives from Erwin 1996 (secondary stress on every second mora preceding the primary); (b) weak roots get 'an epenthetic final vowel which does not affect the stress pattern, so the primary stress on weak roots is antepenultimate (penultimate for pseudo-weak roots, which are underlyingly one syllable long)' (pp.134-135), the same treatment of the weak final syllables -na/-ka/-tra as Erwin's paragogic-vowel stipulation quoted in the entry; (c) 'Other than some stress-bearing prefixes... the only evidence of phonemic stress in the language seems to involve the final syllable' (p.211), which sharpens where the unpredictability sits (final-syllable stress and some prefixes; antepenult vs penult is derived from underlying consonant-final vs vowel-final roots) but keeps stress phonemic for a class of words, so `kind: lexical` stands.

evidence_works.work: Albro 2003, A large-scale, computerized phonological analysis of Malagasy (LSA Annual Meeting paper, UCLA: p.1, p.19)
evidence_works.detail: Precursor of the 2005 dissertation, same analysis. Data: 'the phonological pattern of the Merina dialect (the standard dialect) of Malagasy... based on a large and continually expanding database of Malagasy forms, derived from Hollanger's Malagasy dictionary, data from a native speaker, and several phonological papers (Erwin; Keenan & Razafimamonjy; Keenan & Razafimamonjy; Paul; Keenan & Polinsky)'. Stress summary (p.19, 'The Analysis'): 'Malagasy has right-to-left trochaic stress. Primary stress is final in the word. Stress is phonemic in some words and prefixes. Stress is attracted to heavy syllables (syllables are heavy in Malagasy if they contain a long vowel or a diphthong), sometimes causing a stress clash. Lapse may occur due to phonemic stress in prefixes and also due to avoidance of footing final epenthetic vowels.' Here 'Primary stress is final in the word' means the rightmost of the right-to-left trochaic stresses is primary (2005: 'the rightmost stress of a word having special prominence'), not final-syllable stress. Adds one detail the entry lacks: 'Post-nasal final vowel deletion: Vowels that would otherwise be unstressed are not pronounced after a nasal, although the stress pattern acts as though the vowel is there' (p.19), which refines the weak-final-syllable (-na) point. Agrees with the entry's right-to-left secondary-stress rule, weak-final-syllable treatment and `kind: lexical`.

1585.cfw: The fixed-penult rule rests on Würtz's hedged 1889 missionary sketch, whose own examples (ka-dsá-ri, kambádsi) already put the accent off the penult, whereas Philippson 1991 treats Pokomo as a lexical pitch-accent language with at most one high syllable per word (first stem syllable, penult or final, or none) and only a length peak on the penult, and Nurse 2008 transcribes pairs such as hu-na-gúy-a 'we buy' against hú-na-guy-á 'we will buy' that differ by accent placement alone, so the better reading is lexical accent rather than fixed stress, although Philippson himself calls his Pokomo data thin and doubtful.

1589.prule: No stress or accent rule is stated anywhere in the source (the words 'stress'/'stressed' do not occur in the 169-page article; 'accent' occurs once, about a Proto-Algonquian/Penobscot contrast). What Siebert states is an abstract alternating 'syllabic weight' (heavy vs light) assigned by parity counted from the word's left edge: odd-numbered syllables heavy, even-numbered light, unless the first vowel is weak /e/, in which case even-numbered syllables are heavy. This weight alternation conditions major syncope of weak /e/, /a/ in light closed syllables ending in /s/ or /h/ (never initial/final syllables, never in themes under three syllables). 'Heavy/light' here is a positional (metrical-parity) label, not rime weight (CVV/CVC), and it is never linked to prominence.

1591.prule: Tone-accent system: four contrastive tonal melodies (H, L, HL, LH) on lexical morphemes; at most one H tone per morpheme (culminative), functioning as an accentual prominence; location of H in polysyllabic morphemes is lexically unpredictable; affixes are toneless (default L) and fall under the tone-accent domain of the prosodic head (first lexeme of the word); some words have no H at all. Intensity is explicitly not a marker of word-level prominence. No stress rule by position or weight.

1592.dq: The analysis proposed here to capture word stress assignment in Pulaar is as follows. a) Stress bearing elements are vowels b) Vowels that are head of rhymes are stress bearing. c) The last syllable of the word is marked extrametrical.
1592.dloc: pp. 53-56 (stress patterns and 'Generalizations'), pp. 61-62 (proposed analysis), p. 67 (conclusion)
1592.heavy: Four-way scalar weight: 'CVVC is heavier than CVV which in turn is heavier than CVC which is heavier than CV'; heavy = CVC, CVV, CVVC (earlier authors cited: 'the first heavy syllable (CVV, CVC)').
1592.prule: Final syllable extrametrical (never stressed). Among non-final syllables, main stress goes to the heaviest syllable on the scale CVVC > CVV > CVC > CV; if the competing heavy syllables are of equal weight, the leftmost (first) wins; if no non-final syllable is heavy, stress is initial. Formalised as Halle-Vergnaud bounded left/right-headed constituents built right-to-left with headedness decided by relative syllable 'sonority' (weight).
1592.srule: Secondary stress only on heavy syllables (CVC, CVV, CVVC) that are neither word-final nor adjacent to the main-stressed syllable; hence none in di- and trisyllables, and secondary stresses appear in four- and five-syllable complexes (j'aa taa'r n'aa jo 'person from Jaataar', k'aa sa maa's naa jo 'person from Casamance'). Wiltshire 2006 (after Niang 1997) restates it as 'all other heavy syllables unless clash', with four- to six-syllable examples.

Atonic (軽声) syllables carry no tone, vowel /ə/ only, never utterance-final, rarely word-medial (sesquisyllabic minor syllables); Kato argues their toneless status is phonemic/lexical, explicitly rejecting Phillips (2000)'s view that they are full syllables destressed by position in the phrase/clause. tn.quote: 3. Tonos Se presentan tres tonos fonémicos superficialmente: Alto, Bajo y Ascendente (Bajo-Alto). Los tonos se presentan en la primera columna con vocales modales y en la segunda columna con vocales laringalizadas. Alto wíʧ wich … Bajo tòb tob ‘maguey’ … Ascendente ɾǔʣʲ rudzy … 4. Acento prosódico Las raíces de las palabras de clase mayor se acentúan. El acento prosódico tiene un efecto en la pronunciación de las vocales en ciertos contextos (véase Convenciones). … El tono bajo desciende un poco cuando está antes de pausa: / t ò b / tob ‘maguey’.
tn.translation: 3. Tones. Three phonemic tones occur on the surface: High, Low and Rising (Low-High). The tones are shown in the first column with modal vowels and in the second column with laryngealized vowels. High wíʧ wich … Low tòb tob 'maguey' … Rising ɾǔʣʲ rudzy … 4. Prosodic stress. The roots of major-class words are stressed. Prosodic stress has an effect on the pronunciation of the vowels in certain contexts (see Conventions). … The low tone falls a little when it stands before a pause: /tòb/ tob 'maguey'.

1602.dq: Two levels of stress are exhibited in Old Rapa: word-level stress and phrase-level stress. Both levels play equal and important roles in the functionality of the language. This section first discusses word-level stress in Old Rapa, in both monomorphemic and affixed forms.
1602.dloc: sect. 3.4.1.1 'Primary stress', pp. 61-65; rule preview sect. 3.1.3.1 p. 43; secondary stress sect. 3.4.1.2 pp. 65-66; phrase stress 3.4.2 p. 67
1602.heavy: surface long vowels and surface diphthongs (both long and short) attract stress as a result of their heavier weight; ranked hierarchy (C)ViVi > (C)ViVii > (C)V (long vowel > diphthong > light). Syllables are open ((C)V(V)); no coda weight.
1602.prule: Moraic feet (one heavy or two light syllables) built from the right edge; primary stress on the penultimate mora, i.e. 'stress is on the syllable containing the penultimate mora, unless a long vowel or diphthong is present, in which case stress is on the heavier syllable' (p.43). Refined: (a) primary stress falls on the foot containing the syllable highest on the hierarchy long V > diphthong > light V; (b) if all feet tie, stress falls on the penultimate mora of the second foot from the right. Examples: ivi ['i.vi], puaka [pu.'ɑ.xɑ], tāpū ['tɑ:.pu:], pō'otu ['po:.ʔo.tu], mangavai [mɑ.ŋɑ.'vɑi], 'angai [ʔɑ.'ŋɑi], keiā [kei.'ɑ:].
1602.srule: One secondary stress on the penultimate mora of the leftmost foot (moraic feet built from the right edge), found only in forms of four or more syllables, i.e. affixed forms ('akatika [ˌʔɑ.xɑ.'ti.xɑ], pake'ia [ˌpɑ.xe.'ʔi.ɑ], kite'anga [ˌki.te.'ʔɑ.ŋɑ], 'akaoti'anga [ʔɑ.ˌkao.ti.'ʔɑ.ŋɑ]); stated as tentative ('based on some limited examples, it appears'); no forms longer than five syllables, no alternation described.
1602.quote: Primary stress in Old Rapa is directly related to the relative weight of syllables, where surface long vowels and surface diphthongs (both long and short) attract stress as a result of their heavier weight. Jakarta: Badan Penyelenggara Seri NUSA (published UH 1979 dissertation; Chapters II-IV syntax with numbered word-glossed sentence examples, Chapter V phonology and morphology incl. Table 4 'List of affixes'). Stress statement from McGinn, Richard. 2003. Raising of PMP *a in Bukar-Sadong Land Dayak and Rejang. PL-550:37-64, sect. 2.3 (McGinn 1982 contains no word-stress rule).
morph.rootq: McGinn 2003 §2.3 'Pre-Rejang word stress', p.40: "Nowadays, however, in all contemporary Rejang dialects the stress falls uniformly upon the final syllable of the word." (also p.37: "both Sadong and Rejang are 'oxytone' languages"). The statement is framed on the word, with no reference to root, stem or affixes. McGinn 1982 (the grammar) states no word-stress rule at all; its only prosodic remark is §5.5.5 p.62: pre-stopped final nasals are "coordinated with any rapid change of pitch (rising or lowering) that occurred in the final syllable of the word."
morph.elicq: McGinn 2003 p.40 gives the rule as a bare generalisation inside a historical-phonology argument with no statement of the evidence base: "Nowadays, however, in all contemporary Rejang dialects the stress falls uniformly upon the final syllable of the word. To account for the contemporary data, McGinn (1997) assumed that by the time of Proto Rejang the stress had shifted..."; cf. p.44 on the sister language: "Another assumption is that all contemporary Bukar-Sadong dialects have ultimate stress, again like Rejang; certainly, all those which have been investigated show this pattern." No mention of wordlists, frames, texts or measurements…
morph.stmt: Exclusively prefixing/infixing per the grammar: "Two kinds of affixation are distinguished in Rejang: Prefixation and Infixation. Infixes have already been described as abstract prefixes in 5.3.3." (McGinn 1982 §5.4.3 p.59); all 14 items in Table 4 'List of affixes' (p.60) are prefixes (em-, en-, meng-, peng-, nge-, pe-, be-, te-, ke-1..4, s-1, s-2), the two inflectional ones being "the Oblique Subject affix //en-//, which may be realized as the prefix n- or the infix -en-, and the agentive affix //em-//, which may be realized as m- or -em-" (§5.0 p.54); the only 'suffix' is abstract reduplication ("Doubling is an abstract suffix //DOUBL//", §5.4.2), and articles, possessors, negation…

1604.dq: A masculine noun has penultimate accent, realized as high-low pitch on the last two moras. ... Accent analysis of the verb phrase is, moreover, complicated by its final position in the sentence, where intonation patterns interfere.
1604.prule: Pitch-accent system (Oomen 1981): at most one accented mora per word, realised as high pitch, mora-counting; in basic nouns the accent locus is tied to lexical gender — masculine nouns accent the penultimate mora (H-L over last two moras), feminine nouns the final mora (M-H), the feminine pattern being a lexicalised lost suffix *-et (ínam 'boy' vs inám 'girl'); short-vowel monosyllabic nouns are unaccented (mid pitch). No synchronic stress rule is stated; Oomen reconstructs pre-Rendille word stress bound to penult/antepenult by syllable weight (diachronic only). Sim 1981 (same issue): 'Rendille is tonal'.
1604.srule: None rhythmic: Oomen 1981 treats Rendille as pitch-accent with one accented (high) mora per word and all other pitches derived ('If... the high-pitched mora is located, the pitch of the other moras is predictable'; following moras low, preceding mid). The only 'secondary accent' she reports is morphological: before the accented plural suffix -ó a feminine stem's own accent surfaces as a secondary accent (woró 'wells' mid-high vs worár 'news' low-high).
1604.quote: Rendille clearly makes use of pitch as a prosodic feature. ... In applying these criteria to Rendille, one would interpret the high pitch as stress, not tone. In Rendille one finds monosyllabic words, albeit few, which are only distinguished by a difference in pitch ... Looking at the question diachronically, one may say that present-day Rendille, which at first analysis appears to be a tone language, developed out of a bound stress language, i.e. word stress was bound to the penultimate or antepenultimate, depending on syllable weight. Everything considered it may be best to say, on the line…
1604.idn: Rendille (no dialect named); data: Kenya (informant from Korr, southern Marsabit District), end of 1976 to June 1978; Sim 1981: Nairobi, November 1977, same informant
1604.exq_: In present-day Rendille, basic nouns, except monosyllabics with a short vowel and nouns ending in a vowel, are overtly marked for gender by a different accentual pattern. ... A small number of nouns denoting living beings mark sex by changing the accentual pattern.
1604.tone: Oomen 1981 calls Rendille a pitch-accent language (accent = high pitch on one mora, other pitches predictable; impressionistically also more intensity/length on the accented mora); Sim 1981 p.4: 'Rendille is tonal: little work has been done, however, and in this paper in general only a "prominent-high" is marked for any word.' Pillinger 1988/1989 (via Mous 2021): accentual underlyingly, tonal at the surface (H spreading, contour simplification, downstep), some case forms of nouns carry no H at all; Esser 1991 measured intensity prominence on a low-toned syllable separate from the H — Mous: stress-in-addition-to-tone 'needs further investigation'. No author states a synchronic word-stress placement rule.

1605.heavy: CVC heavier than CV: 'Syllables with a CVC structure are heavier than an element with a CV pattern, and therefore, they become the stress-bearing units in a PWd.' Coda consonants limited to /n/, /h/, /r/ (apical tap); word-final CVC arises only via the enclitics =´in 'INTNS' and =´jj 'AUG' (also CVC in -kwarse 'COND' and Spanish loans such as perduna, suldau). No statement that CVV/diphthongs attract stress (ʔemaina=du is stressed on the penult na, not on mai).
1605.prule: Default: primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word ('in most roots'), realised as high pitch on the stressed syllable and low pitch on the final; stress is computed over the whole phonological word including suffixes/enclitics ('primary stress may move one syllable to the right, depending on the number of morphemes added'). Weight override as stated by the author: a word-final CVC syllable (codas /n h r/; word-final CVC arises only through the enclitics =´in INTNS and =´jj AUG) is heavy and takes primary stress on the final syllable.
1605.srule: Not mentioned in Gallinate Soliz 2020 (sec. 3.2-3.3 pp.12-16, sec. 5 p.19, endnotes 7-8 read): the source speaks only of primary stress; the extra H/M-pitched syllables of trisyllabic+ words (M-H-L, H-H-L) are 'regarded as not being the locus of primary stress despite their acoustic prominence' and are not analysed as secondary stress.

1606.prule: Stress (acento de intensidade) is treated as distinctive: it falls, with no apparent conditioning, on one of the last syllables of the word (Silva 2005 says last four in the text, but fn. 6 says she never recorded it before the antepenult). No weight or fixed-position rule is stated. Reported tendencies differ across sources: Nikulin 2020 (<Lunkes 1967) says position 'parece ser determinada lexicalmente', tending to the penult with some affixes extrametrical and final stress common in probable loans; Silva 2011:151 says in passing 'l'accent tombe en général sur la dernière syllabe'.

1606.cfw: Silva 2005 treats Rikbáktsa stress as unpredictable within the last four syllables and Nikulin 2020, summarizing Lunkes 1967, likewise calls its position lexically determined with a penultimate tendency, but Boswood 1978 and the SIL dictionary (Tremaine 2007) describe regular penultimate stress with suffixes counted, while Silva 2011 and the transcriptions in Pioli 2010 put it on the final syllable, so first-hand descriptions disagree on the very type of system. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Silva 2005 2005.

1607.dq: recent data seems to indicate the existence of contrastive word-level pitch (Kuykendall 2025 p.18); Contrastive high pitch has been observed, even in monosyllabic words (p.45).

1607.prule: No positional word-stress rule is stated in any reachable source. The prosodic contrast described is lexical: an acute-marked 'stressed'/high-pitched vowel distinguishes minimal pairs including monosyllables (gór 'house' vs gor 'gutter', fúl 'flower' vs ful 'bridge', bái 'brother' vs bai 'through'); Kuykendall (2025) reports contrastive word-level (high) pitch and treats the stress-vs-tone/pitch-accent question as unresolved; the Hanifi Rohingya script encodes three tone marks (short-high, long-falling, long-rising).
1607.quote: Kuykendall 2025 p.45: "The acute accent mark is used above vowels in some settings to mark what many have analyzed as contrastive stress and others have called tone. 1607.idn: Rohingya (rhg) of Rakhine State (Arakan), Myanmar, as spoken by refugees/diaspora (Cox's Bazar camps, Bangladesh; United States); no specific dialect; data: Secondary data from the IOM 2022 Rohingya dictionary…
1607.tone: Community/pedagogical sources (Rohingya Language Foundation orthography, Largin & Erden 2019) call the acute-marked vowel 'stressed'; Kuykendall 2025 (the only linguist-authored description reached) says the mark covers 'what many have analyzed as contrastive stress and others have called tone', reports contrastive high pitch on monosyllables and 'contrastive pitch accent', and states no formal suprasegmental analysis exists yet. Hanifi Rohingya Unicode block has three tone marks (U+10D24-10D26: short-high, long-falling, long-rising) which 'indicate stress and vowel length' (r12a). Closest relative Chittagonian is standardly described as tonal. No source gives a default/positional stress rule for unmarked words.
